hook: Before calculators, engineers multiplied big numbers by adding. They looked up the logarithms of the two numbers, added them, and looked up which number had that sum as its logarithm. That trick works because a logarithm turns multiplication into addition, division into subtraction and powers into multiplication.

prereq.why: Multiplying powers of one base adds the exponents.

prereq.q: Multiplying the input of $\log x$ by $100$ does what to the output?

figure.caption: $h(x) = \log_2(4x) = 2 + \log_2 x$: multiplying the input by $4$ is the same as shifting the graph of $\log_2 x$ up $2$.

chain.cause: Exponents add when powers multiply: $b^m b^n = b^{m + n}$
Exponents multiply when a power is raised to a power

chain.effect: change of base: $\log_b x = \frac{\log_a x}{\log_a b}$, so every logarithm is a vertical dilation of every other

ideas: $\log_b(xy) = \log_b x + \log_b y$, $\log_b \frac{x}{y} = \log_b x - \log_b y$, $\log_b(x^n) = n\log_b x$, for $x, y > 0$.
Change of base: $\log_b x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln b}$. So $\log_4 x = \frac{1}{2}\log_2 x$, a vertical dilation.
Graphs: $\log_b(kx) = \log_b k + \log_b x$ is a vertical shift (and a horizontal dilation); $\log_b(x^n) = n\log_b x$ is a vertical dilation.
Watch the domain: $\ln(x^2)$ is defined for $x \ne 0$, but $2\ln x$ only for $x > 0$.

misconception.right: The logarithm of a product is a sum: $\log 2 + \log 3 = \log 6$. There is no rule that splits $\log(x + y)$.

summary: Logarithms turn products into sums, quotients into differences and powers into multiples, because exponents behave that way. Change of base writes any logarithm as a multiple of another, so every logarithmic function is a vertical dilation of every other. On graphs, multiplying the input shifts the graph up or down. Each rule needs positive inputs; watch for domain changes such as $\ln(x^2)$ versus $2\ln x$.
